label: agreeable (Big Five)
source_text: [Table 4.2, conceptual definition of Agreeableness:] Contrasts a prosocial and communal orientation towards others with antagonism and includes traits such as altruism, tender-mindedness, trust, and modesty. [Table 4.3, NEO PI-R facets:] Trust, Straightforwardness, Altruism, Compliance, Modesty, Tender-Mindedness. [Table 4.4, high-pole markers:] Sympathetic, Kind, Appreciative, Affectionate, Soft-hearted, Warm, Generous, Trusting, Helpful, Forgiving, Pleasant, Good-natured, Friendly, Cooperative, Gentle, Unselfish, Praising, Sensitive. [Costa & McCrae, NEO-PI-3 Feedback Summary, A domain:] This domain is concerned with styles of interpersonal interaction. Low scorers are hard-headed and competitive; high scores [sic] compassionate and cooperative.
description_draft: This means taking people at their word and dealing straight, helping before being asked, yielding in a quarrel, saying little of one's own merits, and feeling for anyone who is hurting.
nearest_existing: agreeable (ad-hoc, neg disagreeable): deliberate near-duplicate by rule 5. The ad-hoc file is keeping harmony and avoiding confrontation, i.e. the compliance facet alone; this one carries all six facets (trust, straightforwardness, altruism, compliance, modesty, tender-mindedness). Also near: gentle, trusting, modest, altruistic.
notes: SOURCES FOR ALL TEN BIG FIVE ENTRIES. Primary: John, Naumann & Soto (2008), 'Paradigm shift to the integrative Big Five trait taxonomy: History, measurement, and conceptual issues', Handbook of Personality 3rd ed., authors' manuscript PDF at the source_url (page numbers quoted are the manuscript's: definitions paragraph p. 31, Tables 4.2-4.4 at the end). Its definitions paragraph is word-for-word the John & Srivastava (1999) paragraph the packet names; the 1999 PDF could not be fetched (pages.uoregon.edu/sanjay/pubs/bigfive.pdf and .../bigfive.html now redirect to sanjaysrivastava.com, which 404s; the personality-project.org copy is an image scan with no text layer), and a SlideShare transcript (https://www.slideshare.net/slideshow/bigfive/17475876) confirmed the wording. The NEO-PI-R manual itself is not online; Costa & McCrae's own one-line high/low description of each domain is quoted from PAR's sample 'Your NEO-PI-3 Feedback Summary' (https://www.parinc.com/Portals/0/Webuploads/samplerpts/NEO%20PI-3%20Summary%20PiC.pdf), whose sample client is very high N, very low E, low O, average A and C, so the sample-client sentences quoted under those poles are the publisher's own wording for that range. WebFetch's summarizer refused the PAR PDF on copyright grounds and could not read the chapter PDF, so both were decoded from the raw PDF streams with the project's Python (no file written); digits in the PAR text were lost in decoding, the prose is intact. Everything in source_text outside square brackets is verbatim; the bracketed labels are mine. Both PDFs fetched 2026-10-07.
pair_review: Scope matches facet for facet (trust/suspicion, straightforwardness/manipulation, altruism/self-interest, compliance/fighting, modesty/boasting, tender-mindedness/hard-heartedness); 31 and 31 words. Differences a re-edit might fix: the high's 'helping before being asked' (altruism) has no direct low counterpart, since the low's 'flattering or tricking people into what one wants' covers straightforwardness and self-interest in one clause; the high is written as quiet good conduct, the low as active behaviour toward others, which follows the sources (the low adjectives are the more vivid) but leaves the low pole the more concrete of the two.

label: agreeable (HEXACO)
source_text: Persons with very high scores on the Agreeableness scale forgive the wrongs that they suffered, are lenient in judging others, are willing to compromise and cooperate with others, and can easily control their temper.
description_draft: This means letting go of the wrongs done to one, going easy when judging other people, meeting them halfway to get things done together, and keeping one's temper when provoked.
nearest_existing: forgiving (neg unforgiving) and placid (neg irascible) each take one facet, agreeable (ad-hoc) takes compromise. This one is the HEXACO rotation: forgiveness, gentleness in judging, flexibility and patience, with no trust or altruism content (those sit in Honesty-Humility and Emotionality), so it is not the same as agreeable (Big Five).
notes: hexaco.org fetched cleanly; the page gives the high- and low-scorer sentences for each factor but no adjective lists (the adjectives in the queue's description_notes come from Ashton & Lee's papers, not this page).
pair_review: Facet for facet (forgiveness/grudges, gentleness/fault-finding, flexibility/stubbornness, patience/anger); 30 and 30 words. The low draft sharpens 'feel anger readily in response to mistreatment' into 'flaring up at the smallest slight' while the high keeps the source's level ('keeping one's temper when provoked'); the high's 'to get things done together' adds a purpose clause the low has no equivalent of. Nothing else to flag.

label: antagonistic (Big Five)
source_text: [Table 4.2:] Contrasts a prosocial and communal orientation towards others with antagonism [...] [Table 4.4, low-pole markers:] Fault-finding, Cold, Unfriendly, Quarrelsome, Hard-hearted, Unkind, Cruel, Stern, Thankless, Stingy. [p. 18:] Factor II covers themes such as Tender-mindedness (sensitive, kind, soft-hearted, sympathetic), Altruism (generous, helping, praising), and Trust (trusting, forgiving), as contrasted with Hostility, Criticality, and Distrust. [Costa & McCrae, NEO-PI-3 Feedback Summary, A domain:] Low scorers are hard-headed and competitive [...] [sample-client text, average range:] You are willing at times to flatter or trick people into doing what you want, and you tend to put your own needs and interests before others'. You hold your own in conflicts with others [...] you are hard-headed and tough-minded.
description_draft: This means suspecting everyone of an angle, flattering or tricking people into what one wants, finding fault, fighting every disagreement to win, boasting, and feeling nothing for anyone who is struggling.
nearest_existing: disagreeable (ad-hoc neg of agreeable): contradicting people and letting differences stand, the compliance facet only. hostile and confrontational are the fighting alone, cynical the distrust alone, callous the hard-heartedness alone, manipulative the straightforwardness-low alone. This one is the whole low pole across six facets.
notes: Not marked derived: the sources describe the low scorer by the marker adjectives, by 'Hostility, Criticality, and Distrust', and by Costa & McCrae's 'hard-headed and competitive' plus the flatter-or-trick sentence. 'Boasting' is the one clause with no low-side source word (it inverts the modesty facet). Costa & McCrae frame low A as tough-mindedness as much as hostility; the draft follows the chapter's 'antagonism' and the marker adjectives, which are the harsher reading. 'Antagonism' is Costa & McCrae's own term for the pole, so the queue's label stands. Sources as for agreeable (Big Five).

label: careless (Big Five)
source_text: [Table 4.2, Conscientiousness:] Describes socially prescribed impulse control that facilitates task- and goal-directed behavior, such as thinking before acting, delaying gratification, following norms and rules, and planning, organizing, and prioritizing tasks. [Table 4.4, low-pole markers:] Careless, Disorderly, Frivolous, Irresponsible, Slipshot [sic], Undependable, Forgetful. [Costa & McCrae, NEO-PI-3 Feedback Summary, C domain:] Low scorers are easygoing and not inclined to make plans or schedules. [sample-client text, average range:] You can be sloppy and disorganized, and you are sometimes less dependable and reliable and more likely to bend the rules than you should be. You have limited aspirations and might be considered somewhat lackadaisical or lazy. You sometimes find it difficult to make yourself do what you should, and tend to quit when tasks become too difficult.
description_draft: This means acting on the moment: leaving things in a mess, showing up late or not at all, bending the rules, forgetting promises, and dropping a task once it gets hard.
nearest_existing: careless (ad-hoc, neg of conscientious): deliberate near-duplicate by rule 5. The ad-hoc file is slapdash work, broken deadlines and promises, inattention to detail; this one adds the deliberation and self-discipline facets (acting on impulse, quitting when it gets hard) and disorder. Also near: irresponsible, sloppy, impulsive, lazy.
notes: Costa & McCrae's low-C sentence is mild ('easygoing and not inclined to make plans or schedules'); the vice-level wording rests on the marker adjectives and on the sample-client sentences, which are average-range text but low-side in content. Not marked derived for that reason; 'acting on the moment' inverts the definition's 'thinking before acting'. Costa & McCrae's own name for the low pole is 'lack of direction' (per the queue), not 'careless'. Sources as for agreeable (Big Five).
pair_review: Same scope (order, punctuality, duty and rules, effort, deliberation); 29 and 31 words. The high opens with a two-part gloss ('thinking before acting and putting the task before the pleasure'), the low with a one-part gloss ('acting on the moment'). The high's 'aiming high' (achievement striving) and 'checking the work twice' (competence) answer the low's 'dropping a task once it gets hard' and 'leaving things in a mess' only loosely; 'bending the rules' (from Costa & McCrae's text) has a direct high counterpart in 'honoring every obligation'.

label: careless (HEXACO)
source_text: Conversely, persons with very low scores on this scale tend to be unconcerned with orderly surroundings or schedules, avoid difficult tasks or challenging goals, are satisfied with work that contains some errors, and make decisions on impulse or with little reflection.
description_draft: This means leaving the desk a mess and the calendar blank, steering clear of hard tasks and ambitious goals, handing in work with mistakes in it, and deciding on impulse.
nearest_existing: careless (ad-hoc) and careless (Big Five) are the twins by design; this one follows the HEXACO facets (organization, diligence, perfectionism, prudence), so it has no duty, rules or punctuality content and adds avoiding hard goals and tolerating errors. Also near: sloppy, lazy, impulsive, disorganized.
notes: hexaco.org's low-scorer sentence itself carries the hedge 'tend to be'; dropped in the draft per the rules.
pair_review: Facet for facet (organization, diligence, perfectionism, prudence); 30 and 30 words; both open on the desk-and-calendar image, which a re-edit could vary. The low is harder than its source ('unconcerned with orderly surroundings or schedules' became 'leaving the desk a mess and the calendar blank') while the high stays at the source's level. The high's 'grinding steadily toward a goal' is effort, the low's 'steering clear of hard tasks and ambitious goals' is avoidance of difficulty, which is the source's own asymmetry.

label: closed (Big Five)
source_text: [Table 4.2, Openness:] Describes the breadth, depth, originality, and complexity of an individual's mental and experiential life. [p. 31:] Openness to Experience (vs. closed-mindedness) [...] [Table 4.4, low-pole markers:] Commonplace, Narrow interests, Simple, Shallow, Unintelligent. [Costa & McCrae, NEO-PI-3 Feedback Summary, O domain:] Low scorers are down-to-earth and conventional; they prefer the familiar and the tried-and-true. [sample-client text, low range:] Your responses suggest that you are generally closed. You consider daydreaming and fantasy a waste of time, and have a limited imagination. [...] You seldom enjoy new and different activities and have a low need for variety in your life. You are not interested in intellectual pursuits for their own sake and you are conservative in your social, political, and moral beliefs.
description_draft: This means sticking to the tried-and-true: calling daydreams a waste of time, shrugging at art, paying feelings no mind, ordering the usual, leaving ideas to others, and keeping one's inherited beliefs.
nearest_existing: closed_minded (neg of open_minded) is refusing to weigh contrary views, one facet (ideas/values) in an epistemic key; unadventurous is the actions facet, philistine and prosaic the aesthetics facet, traditional and conservative the values facet. This one spans all six Openness facets as a temperament, not a debating stance. The queue's low-pole word 'closed' is confirmed by Costa & McCrae's own feedback text ('you are generally closed').
notes: Five of the six clauses have direct low-side source sentences; the aesthetics clause ('shrugging at art') rests on the markers (Commonplace, Shallow) and the definition, because the feedback summary's art sentence was average-range for the sample client. Sources as for agreeable (Big Five).
pair_review: Both drafts run through the six facets in the same order (fantasy, aesthetics, feelings, actions, ideas, values), 31 words each, so they read as mirror images. This came from each pole's own source (the feedback-summary low-O paragraph lists exactly these six) rather than from forcing, but Roger may want one of them re-ordered or re-imaged to loosen the parallel. The high carries the mandated gloss 'open to experience'; the low's gloss is Costa & McCrae's phrase 'the tried-and-true'. The low's aesthetics clause ('shrugging at art') is thinner than the high's ('being moved by music and art').

label: conscientious (Big Five)
source_text: [Table 4.2:] Describes socially prescribed impulse control that facilitates task- and goal-directed behavior, such as thinking before acting, delaying gratification, following norms and rules, and planning, organizing, and prioritizing tasks. [Table 4.3, NEO PI-R facets:] Competence, Order, Dutifulness, Achievement Striving, Self-Discipline, Deliberation. [Table 4.4, high-pole markers:] Organized, Thorough, Planful, Efficient, Responsible, Reliable, Dependable, Conscientious, Precise, Practical, Deliberate, Painstaking, Cautious. [Table 4.2, behavioral examples:] Arrive early or on time for appointments; Study hard in order to get the highest grade in class; Double-check a term paper for typing and spelling errors. [Costa & McCrae, NEO-PI-3 Feedback Summary, C domain:] Traits in this domain describe differences in motivation and persistence. [...] High scorers are conscientious and well organized.
description_draft: This means thinking before acting and putting the task before the pleasure: keeping things in order, arriving on time, honoring every obligation, aiming high, and checking the work twice.
nearest_existing: conscientious (ad-hoc, neg careless): deliberate near-duplicate by rule 5. The ad-hoc file is thoroughness, diligence, reliability and attention to detail (work habits); this one adds the deliberation and self-discipline facets (thinking before acting, delaying gratification) and dutifulness. Also near: self_disciplined, responsible, methodical, dependable.

label: conscientious (HEXACO)
source_text: Persons with very high scores on the Conscientiousness scale organize their time and their physical surroundings, work in a disciplined way toward their goals, strive for accuracy and perfection in their tasks, and deliberate carefully when making decisions.
description_draft: This means keeping one's desk, calendar and plans in order, grinding steadily toward a goal, polishing work until it is exactly right, and weighing a decision carefully before making it.
nearest_existing: conscientious (ad-hoc) and conscientious (Big Five) are the twins by design; this one follows the HEXACO facets (organization, diligence, perfectionism, prudence), so it drops duty, rules and punctuality and adds perfectionism outright. Also near: methodical, perfectionist, deliberate, industrious.

label: conventional (HEXACO)
source_text: Conversely, persons with very low scores on this scale are rather unimpressed by most works of art, feel little intellectual curiosity, avoid creative pursuits, and feel little attraction toward ideas that may seem radical or unconventional.
description_draft: This means walking past most art unmoved, feeling no itch to learn for its own sake, leaving painting, writing and invention to others, and finding radical ideas more off-putting than interesting.
nearest_existing: conventional (plain, neg eccentric) is reaching for the standard answer and distrusting what would stand out, a style of doing; this one is a temperament across the four HEXACO Openness facets (unmoved by art, incurious, uncreative, cool to radical ideas). Also near: philistine, incurious, closed (Big Five). The shared word is the collision the queue already flags.
notes: hexaco.org's hedges ('rather unimpressed', 'may seem') dropped in the draft.
pair_review: Facet for facet (aesthetic appreciation, inquisitiveness, creativity, unconventionality); 31 and 32 words. The high's 'wanting to know how everything works' is broader than the source's 'inquisitive about various domains of knowledge', and its low counterpart 'feeling no itch to learn for its own sake' echoes Costa & McCrae's Big Five wording ('intellectual pursuits for their own sake') rather than hexaco.org's 'little intellectual curiosity'. The high keeps the source's 'unusual ideas or people' ('strange ideas and odd people'); the low drops people ('radical ideas' only), as its own source does. The high's imagery (painting, landscape, ordinary day) is richer than the low's.

label: emotional (HEXACO)
source_text: Persons with very high scores on the Emotionality scale experience fear of physical dangers, experience anxiety in response to life's stresses, feel a need for emotional support from others, and feel empathy and sentimental attachments with others.
description_draft: This means flinching from physical danger, worrying hard when life gets stressful, needing a shoulder to lean on, and forming deep, tender attachments to people, feeling their pain as one's own.
nearest_existing: emotional (ad-hoc, neg non-emotional) is acknowledging and discussing feelings, an expressive style; the name match is the deliberate near-duplicate the packet mentions, but the content differs: this one is the HEXACO factor (fearfulness, anxiety, dependence, sentimentality). Also near: anxious, timid, clingy, dependent, sentimental, empathetic. Not neurotic (Big Five): no anger, depression or impulsiveness; dependence and sentimentality instead.
pair_review: Facet for facet (fearfulness, anxiety, dependence, sentimentality with empathy); 31 and 30 words. The high spends two clauses on the fourth facet ('forming deep, tender attachments', 'feeling their pain as one's own') where the low has one ('holding people at arm's length', which the low's source gives as 'feel emotionally detached from others'; the word 'emotional' was kept out of the low draft because it is the partner's label); the low spends two on dependence ('keeping one's troubles to oneself', 'asking no one for support') where the high has one. Both follow their source sentences, which are uneven the same way.

label: emotionally-stable (Big Five)
source_text: [Table 4.2, Neuroticism:] Contrasts emotional stability and even-temperedness with negative emotionality, such as feeling anxious, nervous, sad, and tense. [Table 4.4, low-pole markers:] Stable, Calm, Contented. [Table 4.2, behavioral examples, reverse-keyed:] Accept the good and the bad in my life without complaining or bragging (R); Take it easy and relax. (R) [Costa & McCrae, NEO-PI-3 Feedback Summary, N domain:] Traits in the N domain reflect different ways of reacting emotionally to distressing circumstances. Low scorers are resilient, rarely experiencing negative emotions.
description_draft: This means staying calm and even-tempered: taking bad news in stride, slow to anger, quick to shake off gloom, unembarrassed in company, passing up temptations, and steady under stress.
nearest_existing: even_tempered (neg temperamental), 'taking either kind of news in stride, with no moods to brace for', is the closest single file; calm, composed, unflappable, placid, resilient and self_assured each take one facet; neurotic's ad-hoc neg is composed. This one is the whole low pole of Neuroticism: the six facets reversed (anxiety, anger, depression, self-consciousness, impulsiveness, vulnerability).
notes: Marked derived: the sources give the low pole only as labels ('emotional stability and even-temperedness'), three adjectives (Stable, Calm, Contented), two reverse-keyed items and Costa & McCrae's one sentence ('resilient, rarely experiencing negative emotions'), so the six behaviours are the Neuroticism facets written as their opposites. Goldberg's name for the factor is Emotional Stability (per the queue), which the label follows. Sources as for agreeable (Big Five).
pair_review: Both drafts run the six facets in the same order; 29 and 29 words. The high is all actions ('fretting', 'snapping', 'sinking', 'flushing', 'giving in', 'going to pieces'); the low mixes participles with adjectives ('slow to anger', 'unembarrassed', 'steady'), so the low reads as a state and the high as conduct. The low carries a gloss ('staying calm and even-tempered') the high lacks (cut for length). 'Passing up temptations' answers 'giving in to cravings' almost word for word, the one place the inversion is exact.

label: extraverted (Big Five)
source_text: [Table 4.2, Extraversion:] Implies an energetic approach toward the social and material world and includes traits such as sociability, activity, assertiveness, and positive emotionality. [Table 4.3, NEO PI-R facets:] Warmth, Gregariousness, Assertiveness, Activity, Excitement-Seeking, Positive emotions. [Table 4.4, high-pole markers:] Talkative, Assertive, Active, Energetic, Outgoing, Outspoken, Dominant, Forceful, Enthusiastic, Show-off, Sociable, Spunky, Adventurous, Noisy, Bossy. [Table 4.2, behavioral examples:] Approach strangers at a party and introduce myself; Take the lead in organizing a project. [Costa & McCrae, NEO-PI-3 Feedback Summary, E domain:] The E domain measures traits related to energy and enthusiasm, especially when dealing with people. Low scorers are serious and introverted; high scorers are outgoing extraverts.
description_draft: This means going at the world with energy: walking up to strangers at a party, taking the lead in a group, keeping busy, chasing excitement, and bubbling with warmth and good cheer.
nearest_existing: extroverted (ad-hoc, spelled with o, neg introverted): deliberate near-duplicate by rule 5. The ad-hoc file is the energized-by-company mechanism (seeking people out, speaking in groups, preferring a crowd); this one carries the six facets, adding assertiveness, activity, excitement-seeking and positive emotions. Also near: gregarious, energetic, cheerful, bold.
notes: The standard's spelling 'extraverted' is kept (the ad-hoc trait is extroverted). At the 32-word ceiling. Sources as for agreeable (Big Five).
pair_review: Same scope (sociability, assertiveness, activity, excitement-seeking, positive emotion; warmth on the high side, 'formal and distant' on the low); 32 and 29 words. The high is a string of actions, the low a string of states ('formal and distant', 'silent', 'serious', 'slow-paced'); the high's gloss is the definition ('going at the world with energy'), the low's a scene ('keeping to the edge of the room'). Costa & McCrae's low-E text is the richer source, so the low pole stands on more source wording than the high; a re-edit could give the low pole verbs or the high pole a scene.

label: extraverted (HEXACO)
source_text: Persons with very high scores on the Extraversion scale feel positively about themselves, feel confident when leading or addressing groups of people, enjoy social gatherings and interactions, and experience positive feelings of enthusiasm and energy.
description_draft: This means liking who one is, stepping up to lead or address a crowd without a flutter, loving a party and a good talk, and running on enthusiasm and energy.
nearest_existing: extroverted (ad-hoc) and extraverted (Big Five) are the twins by design; this one follows the HEXACO facets (social self-esteem, social boldness, sociability, liveliness), so it opens on self-regard ('liking who one is') and has no warmth, activity or excitement-seeking content. Also near: self_assured, confident, gregarious, cheerful.
pair_review: Facet for facet (social self-esteem, social boldness, sociability, liveliness); 30 and 31 words. The low's last clause is comparative ('less bounce and hope than the people around'), following the source's 'less lively and optimistic than others do', where the high is absolute ('running on enthusiasm and energy'); the low's third clause is indifference ('shrugging off invitations') where the high is enjoyment, again as in the source. 'Liking who one is' and 'thinking oneself unpopular' are not exact opposites (self-regard versus perceived popularity), the source's own asymmetry.

label: honest-humble (HEXACO)
source_text: Persons with very high scores on the Honesty-Humility scale avoid manipulating others for personal gain, feel little temptation to break rules, are uninterested in lavish wealth and luxuries, and feel no special entitlement to elevated social status.
description_draft: This means dealing straight with people rather than working them for gain, keeping to the rules even when cheating would pay, caring nothing for riches and luxury, and claiming no special standing.
nearest_existing: No single corpus trait covers it. Closest: modest ('claiming no special insight or importance'), fair ('refusing any edge gained by cheating'), honest and sincere (truth-telling rather than non-manipulation), and the negatives of greedy and entitled. This is the genuinely new axis: sincerity, fairness, greed avoidance and modesty as one disposition.
pair_review: Facet for facet (sincerity, fairness, greed avoidance, modesty); 32 and 29 words. The high is written as four restraints ('rather than working them', 'even when cheating would pay', 'caring nothing for', 'claiming no'), which follows the source (all four of its clauses are avoidances) but risks reading as an absence beside the low's four active behaviours; the high's sincerity clause also carries a 'rather than' contrast the low has none of. A re-edit could give the high pole positive conduct (paying what is owed, giving credit, living plainly) if Roger wants it to stand on its own.

label: introverted (Big Five)
source_text: [Table 4.4, low-pole markers:] Quiet, Reserved, Shy, Silent, Withdrawn, Retiring. [Table 4.2, reverse-keyed example:] Keep quiet when I disagree with others (R). [Costa & McCrae, NEO-PI-3 Feedback Summary, E domain:] Low scorers are serious and introverted; high scorers are outgoing extraverts. [sample-client text, very low range:] You are somewhat formal and distant in your relationships with others and you rarely enjoy large and noisy crowds or parties. You are reluctant to assert yourself and prefer to stay in the background in meetings and group discussions. You have a low level of energy and prefer a slow and steady pace. Excitement, stimulation, and thrills have little appeal to you and you are less prone to experience feelings of joy and happiness than most women.
description_draft: This means keeping to the edge of the room: formal and distant with people, out of noisy crowds and parties, silent in meetings, serious, slow-paced, and unmoved by thrills.
nearest_existing: introverted (ad-hoc, neg extroverted): deliberate near-duplicate by rule 5. The ad-hoc file is the drained-by-company mechanism (keeping to oneself, needing time alone after social occasions); this one is the six facets reversed per Costa & McCrae's low-E text, adding unassertiveness, low energy and no taste for thrills. Also near: reserved, solitary, timid, unassuming.
notes: Not marked derived: all six clauses have direct source sentences in Costa & McCrae's very-low-E feedback text ('formal and distant', 'noisy crowds or parties', 'stay in the background in meetings', 'serious', 'slow and steady pace', 'thrills have little appeal'). The sample client is female, hence 'than most women' in the source. Sources as for agreeable (Big Five).

label: introverted (HEXACO)
source_text: Conversely, persons with very low scores on this scale consider themselves unpopular, feel awkward when they are the center of social attention, are indifferent to social activities, and feel less lively and optimistic than others do.
description_draft: This means thinking oneself unpopular, squirming when all eyes turn one's way, shrugging off invitations and gatherings, and going through the day with less bounce and hope than the people around.
nearest_existing: introverted (ad-hoc) and introverted (Big Five) are the twins by design; this one follows the HEXACO facets reversed (low social self-esteem, social awkwardness, indifference to company, low liveliness), so it opens on self-regard. Also near: unpopular, self_conscious, solitary, insecure.

label: neurotic (Big Five)
source_text: [Table 4.2:] Contrasts emotional stability and even-temperedness with negative emotionality, such as feeling anxious, nervous, sad, and tense. [Table 4.3, NEO PI-R facets:] Anxiety, Angry Hostility, Depression, Self-Consciousness, Impulsiveness, Vulnerability. [Table 4.4, high-pole markers:] Tense, Anxious, Nervous, Moody, Worrying, Touchy, Fearful, High-strung, Self-pitying, Temperamental, Unstable, Self-punishing, Despondent, Emotional. [Costa & McCrae, NEO-PI-3 Feedback Summary, N domain, sample-client text, very high range:] you are anxious, generally apprehensive, and prone to worry. You often feel frustrated, irritable, and angry at others and you are prone to feeling sad, lonely, and dejected. Embarrassment or shyness when dealing with people, especially strangers, is often a problem for you. You report being poor at controlling your impulses and desires and you are unable to handle stress well.
description_draft: This means fretting over what could go wrong, snapping at people, sinking into sadness, flushing with embarrassment in company, giving in to cravings, and going to pieces under stress.
nearest_existing: neurotic (ad-hoc, neg composed): deliberate near-duplicate by rule 5. The ad-hoc file is anxiety, worry, instability and reactivity in abstract nouns; this one is the six facets as behaviour, adding anger, depression, self-consciousness and impulsiveness. Also near: anxious, irascible, melancholic, self_conscious, impulsive, fragile. Rotated cousin of emotional (HEXACO): anger stays here, dependence and sentimentality do not.

label: open (Big Five)
source_text: [p. 31:] Openness to Experience (vs. closed-mindedness) describes the breadth, depth, originality, and complexity of an individual's mental and experiential life. [Table 4.3, NEO PI-R facets:] Fantasy, Aesthetics, Feelings, Actions, Ideas, Values. [Table 4.4, high-pole markers:] Wide interests, Imaginative, Intelligent, Original, Insightful, Curious, Sophisticated, Artistic, Clever, Inventive, Sharp-witted, Ingenious, Witty, Resourceful, Wise. [Table 4.2, behavioral examples:] Take the time to learn something simply for the joy of learning; Watch documentaries or educational TV; Come up with novel set-ups for my living space; Look for stimulating activities that break up my routine. [Costa & McCrae, NEO-PI-3 Feedback Summary, O domain:] The facets of this domain measure responses to various kinds of experience. [...] High scorers are imaginative and open-minded.
description_draft: This means being open to experience: daydreaming freely, being moved by music and art, savoring one's feelings, trying the unfamiliar, chewing on ideas for their own sake, and questioning inherited values.
nearest_existing: open_minded (neg closed-minded) is hearing out a contrary view and changing one's mind, one facet (ideas/values) in an epistemic key; curious and inquisitive are the ideas facet, aesthete and artistic the aesthetics facet, adventurous and adventurous_eater the actions facet, creative the fantasy facet. This one is the whole six-facet domain; the suffix keeps it apart from open_ended and transparent, as the queue notes.
notes: Opens with 'open to experience' as the queue's description_notes require; the label 'open' plus this qualifier is the sense-picking opening rule 1 allows. Sources as for agreeable (Big Five).

label: open (HEXACO)
source_text: Persons with very high scores on the Openness to Experience scale become absorbed in the beauty of art and nature, are inquisitive about various domains of knowledge, use their imagination freely in everyday life, and take an interest in unusual ideas or people.
description_draft: This means losing oneself in a painting or a landscape, wanting to know how everything works, letting imagination run through an ordinary day, and being drawn to strange ideas and odd people.
nearest_existing: open (Big Five) is the twin by design; this one follows the four HEXACO facets (aesthetic appreciation, inquisitiveness, creativity, unconventionality), so it has no feelings or values content and leans to art, nature and oddity. Also near: aesthete, curious, creative, eccentric, absorption_prone.

label: quarrelsome (HEXACO)
source_text: Conversely, persons with very low scores on this scale hold grudges against those who have harmed them, are rather critical of others' shortcomings, are stubborn in defending their point of view, and feel anger readily in response to mistreatment.
description_draft: This means nursing a grudge against anyone who has done one wrong, picking at other people's faults, refusing to budge in an argument, and flaring up at the smallest slight.
nearest_existing: irascible (neg placid) is the anger facet, unforgiving the grudge facet, unyielding the stubbornness facet, judgmental the fault-finding facet; confrontational and disagreeable are near but about seeking or standing in conflict. This one is the four together. Not antagonistic (Big Five): no distrust, manipulation or hard-heartedness here, those sit in Honesty-Humility and Emotionality.
notes: hexaco.org's 'rather critical' hedge dropped; 'feel anger readily in response to mistreatment' sharpened to 'flaring up at the smallest slight' for the vice pole (flagged in the pair review on agreeable (HEXACO)).

label: sly (HEXACO)
source_text: Conversely, persons with very low scores on this scale will flatter others to get what they want, are inclined to break rules for personal profit, are motivated by material gain, and feel a strong sense of self-importance.
description_draft: This means flattering people to get what one wants, breaking a rule whenever it pays, chasing money and luxury, and carrying oneself as someone who matters more than others.
nearest_existing: manipulative, scheming and deceitful are the sincerity facet; rule_breaking and unfair the fairness facet; greedy and materialistic the greed facet; arrogant, grandiose, entitled and self_aggrandizing the modesty facet. No single file has the four together; this is the dark core the queue describes. 'Sly' is the first of Ashton & Lee's low adjectives; the description carries the whole pole, not cunning alone.
notes: The source's 'are inclined to' and 'are motivated by' are rendered as outright behaviour ('breaking a rule whenever it pays', 'chasing money and luxury'), per the vice rule.

label: tough (HEXACO)
source_text: Conversely, persons with very low scores on this scale are not deterred by the prospect of physical harm, feel little worry even in stressful situations, have little need to share their concerns with others, and feel emotionally detached from others.
description_draft: This means walking toward physical danger without a second thought, staying unworried under pressure, keeping one's troubles to oneself, asking no one for support, and holding people at arm's length.
nearest_existing: No plain 'tough' file exists in the corpus yet (the queue says one is approved as nurturing's partner, so a name collision is coming). Closest existing: stoic (calm composure and emotional restraint), brave (feeling the fear and going ahead), self_reliant (asking nobody for help), detached and unsentimental (emotional distance), thick_skinned. This one is the four Emotionality facets reversed: fearless, unworried, independent, detached. Hofstede's tough/tender (from the queue) is close in sense.
notes: Overlap with the planned plain tough: that one will be the opposite of nurturing (hard on people), this one is low Emotionality (hard in oneself); worth checking the two descriptions side by side when the plain one is drafted. 'Not deterred by the prospect of physical harm' became 'walking toward physical danger without a second thought', a shade past the source.
